item.title: Student voice systems have transformed beyond recognition
item.description: Ashley Storer-Smith outlines findings from a sector-wide review of student representation systems, highlighting recent changes in structure, recruitment, and practice

item.title: Demonstrating the benefit of research is key to universities maintaining their social license
item.description: As part of the commission for better economic growth Joan Concannon sets out the geographic, social, and economic failures of the research investment landscape

item.title: The graduate premium in a world of human capital
item.description: It turns out there are other bits of government beyond DfE with an interest in graduate earnings. David Kernohan unexpectedly finds hope in neoclassical economic theory

item.title: More AI will not beat the Red Queen
item.description: The past few months have seen a crescendo of commentary highlighting threats to academic quality review, not least from the effects of GenAI use. In this article, Neil Jacobs, Natasha Mauther, Peter Flach and Marcus Munafò suggest that the stakes may be higher – and the solutions more radical – than many expect.

item.title: AI enforcement apparatus exists to punish the anxious middle
item.description: Detection tools miss the determined cheaters and terrify the principled non-users into self-censoring their own punctuation. Jim Dickinson makes the case for accountability moments over algorithmic guesswork

item.title: Trained to stop learning: How students are experiencing assessment and learning in an age of AI
item.description: New research from Wonkhe finds that assessment design – not AI policy – is what determines whether students use AI to learn or to produce. Jim Dickinson and Mack Marshall explain

item.title: Disengaged AI use is a symptom of the structural squeeze on choice
item.description: As universities cut optional modules to balance the books, Mack Marshall finds that restricted choice is one of the clearest correlates of disengaged AI use

item.title: AI policy is penalising the students most trying to comply
item.description: Jim Dickinson presents findings from new research on students' use of AI – and argues the sector is punishing precisely the disposition it should be cultivating

item.title: Students should take risks, but not with their lives
item.description: Student activities are sold as employability development – and they are. Dawn Lees warns that without proper risk assessment culture and trained student leaders, the consequences can be fatal

item.title: Group essays? Pull the other one
item.description: An Australian politician's call to abolish group assignments has drawn ridicule, but Jim Dickinson finds students' frustrations are well-founded – and the fixes already exist
